課程目標與學習成效:
This course is a required foundational course for all students at the International College of Innovation. It introduces students to the essential statistical tools and shows how they are used to analyze quantitative data. A fundamental understanding of these tools is a critical foundation for scientific research. This course is designed mainly as AI-mediated learning, which means that you, as a student, will be responsible for learning key concepts and skills most of the time using an AI tool of your preference, guided by a prepared list of questions for each session. The instructor and TAs will be facilitators to help you learn.
The course covers descriptive statistics, inference from samples, hypothesis testing, and various basic statistical analyses. The course will also introduce R, a free software for statistical computing and graphics. You will need to bring a laptop or notebook to the class to use R. We will have practice time to use R almost every week.
Upon successful completion of this course, you will be able to complete the following tasks:
1. Explain basic concepts of social statistics (e.g., population vs. sample, sampling distribution).
2. Summarize numeric data by computing descriptive statistics (e.g., mean, variance) and creating tables and graphs. For each procedure, you will learn a hand calculation method (using calculators) and a computer method (using software such as R).
3. Compute various inferential statistics (e.g., t-score) using hand calculation and computer methods.
4. Apply probability theory to test research hypotheses.
5. Explain the differences among various statistical techniques and identify an appropriate method for a given set of variables and research questions.

This course introduces the full process of data science, from collecting raw data to building useful insights and models. Students will learn how to gather data from sources like websites and APIs, clean and prepare it for analysis, and label image or text data when needed. The course covers key steps in data science, including data wrangling, exploration, visualization, modeling, and evaluation.
In the image section, students will learn how to label and explore image data, apply clustering techniques like K-means to group visual patterns, and understand how to move from basic clustering to using pre-trained models for classification. For each method, students will learn how to evaluate performance using metrics such as accuracy and Intersection over Union (IoU).
In the text section, the course begins with text cleaning and basic techniques like TF-IDF. Students will then explore more powerful models like BERT, and learn how different models can be used for classification and language understanding tasks. Along the way, students will compare results using standard evaluation metrics.
Rather than focusing only on model training, this course emphasizes how to use data to answer real questions, communicate findings, and build end-to-end data science workflows. Students will use Python tools such as Pandas, Scikit-learn, Matplotlib, and Hugging Face Transformers to work on real datasets and complete hands-on projects.
This course is designed for students with basic Python and AI knowledge who want to deepen their understanding of the data science pipeline.
課程目標與學習成效: This course aims to help students understand the full process of data science, from collecting and preparing data to building and evaluating models. Students will learn how to handle different types of data, including text and images, and apply both basic and advanced techniques such as K-means clustering, TF-IDF, and classification. By the end of the course, students will be able to use Python tools to explore data, label datasets, apply machine learning models, and evaluate results using metrics like accuracy and IoU. They will also complete a small project to apply what they have learned in a real-world context.

This course introduces students to the sociological study of technoscience and society. You will explore and analyze what it means to live in a contemporary technological society. In this part, you will investigate and unravel this distinctive condition. You will study different areas where questions about technology’s role in society are central: economy, transportation, and corporations. In this course, you will learn that technological development is not just about technology.

課程簡介:
I. Course Objectives
This course is designed to help students understand the legal and governance issues arising from the development of digital technologies, with data governance as its central focus. It addresses major emerging topics, including personal data protection, artificial intelligence governance, digital platform accountability, open government data, data sharing, cybersecurity, cross-border data flows, and the European Union(EU)’s data governance framework.
Taught entirely in English, the course introduces students to core concepts in contemporary international technology law. It examines legal issues that arise throughout the data life cycle, from collection, processing, use, retention, and sharing to deletion. The course also considers the legality of artificial intelligence systems in model training and content generation, and analyzes the respective responsibilities and obligations of governments, businesses, digital platforms, and data intermediaries in data governance.
The course further incorporates Taiwan’s legal framework, the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Data Governance Act, Data Act, Artificial Intelligence Act, and other significant legislative developments and international trends. Through this comparative approach, students will develop a stronger interest in technology law and acquire the analytical skills needed to address practical legal issues.
II. Course Description
This course begins with legal issues related to data use as an entry point into technology law. It introduces key legal concepts, including personal data protection, informational self-determination, privacy, and data governance, before moving to issues such as open government data, data sharing, data intermediary services, data altruism, data access for Internet of Things devices and connected products, cloud switching, regulation of artificial intelligence technologies, algorithmic transparency, disclosure obligations, and legal requirements for cross-border data transfers.
The course focuses on recent developments in the EU’s data governance regime and explains how the GDPR, Data Governance Act, Data Act, and Artificial Intelligence Act together shape a technology law framework grounded in trustworthiness, data access, and risk management. In addition to introducing major international technology laws, the course includes weekly case discussions to help students examine the relationship between data governance, personal data protection, public interest, industrial innovation, digital market competition, national data sovereignty, and the protection of fundamental rights.
課程目標與學習成效:
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:
Understand the foundational theories and regulatory structure of technology law and data governance.
Examine legal issues concerning personal data protection, data sharing, digital platform regulation, risk-based regulation of artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity safeguards.
Compare Taiwan’s digital legal framework with the GDPR, Data Governance Act, Data Act, and other major technology laws of the EU.
Assess, from legal and governance perspectives, personal data protection risks and appropriate levels of regulatory oversight arising from artificial intelligence and other technological applications.
Analyze current disputes and cases involving the application of technology law from an independent perspective and propose appropriate legal or policy reforms.

115-1課表備註: 英文授課
課程簡介:
This course examines the rise of China as the defining force shaping politics and society across the Greater China region. Over the past four decades, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has transformed from a poor, isolated polity into the world’s second-largest economy and a leading geopolitical power — with profound consequences not only for its own governance but for its relationship with Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan, three societies bound to the mainland by deep cultural and historical ties yet possessing distinct institutional inheritances. The course asks: how has China’s rise reshaped the political institutions, social fabric, and external relationships of each of these polities, and what does the resulting variation tell us about the reach and the limits of Chinese-style governance?
The first half of the course maps the mainland system that drives these dynamics: major theoretical traditions for understanding Chinese politics (authoritarian resilience, fragmented and consultative authoritarianism, adaptive governance, party-state institutionalism); the organisation, ideology, and cadre system of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) under Xi Jinping; political change and policy implementation under the post-2012 leadership; the social transformation generated by urbanisation, hukou reform, demographic change, and growing inequality; and state–society relations including civil society, religion, ethnic politics, surveillance, and platform politics.
The second half traces how the rise of China has reshaped — and is being reshaped by — its peripheries. In Hong Kong, the asymmetric integration of the Special Administrative Region into the mainland’s political and economic order has accelerated since 2014, culminating in the 2020 National Security Law, the 2021 “patriots-only” electoral overhaul, and the 2024 Safeguarding National Security Ordinance (Article 23). In Macau, the rise of China has been managed through a quieter politics of accommodation, with deepening integration into the Greater Bay Area and continued reliance on a gaming economy increasingly aligned with Beijing’s strategic priorities. In Taiwan, China’s rise has driven both deepening economic interdependence (trade, investment, ECFA, semiconductors) and an intensifying security competition, with democratisation, identity politics, the 2024 presidential election, and the role of the United States all shaping the cross-Strait equation. The final two weeks are reserved for student case presentations.
課程目標與學習成效: By the end of the course, students should be able to: (1) compare leading theoretical models of Chinese governance and assess their analytical reach; (2) explain how the CCP organises power and recruits, monitors, and disciplines cadres; (3) trace the principal directions of political change under Xi Jinping; (4) analyse social transformation and state–society contention in mainland China; (5) compare the post-handover political trajectories of Hong Kong and Macau; (6) account for the trajectory of Taiwan’s democratisation and cross-Strait relations; and (7) deliver a research-grade case study and reflection note that engage critically with primary scholarship.

課程簡介:
Course Description
This course has two aims. On one hand, It intends to help ICI (International College of Innovation) students acquire basic knowledge of sustainability reporting and carbon accounting. These are two popular tools in the corporate world of sustainability and in the field of environmental governance. On the other hand, this course also aims to equip ICI students with critical and historical perspective to understand the quantification logic behind the current trend of global environmental governance.
This course interweaves technical training and critical analysis throughout the semester: you will read sustainability reports learn the standards behind them, examine how metrics are constructed, and learn directly from practitioners’ insights. Specifically, this course collaborates NCCU's own Sustainability Office. We will use NCCU’s own Sustainability Report as a companion case and interact with the authors who craft the report from office. Furthermore, we will use the global higher education sector as our focus and collectively analyze how different universities develop their own Sustainability Reports and what the implications are.
Course Format
Class Activity & Group Discussion & Short Lecture:
I employ a
student-centered learning approach
in this course rather than a traditional lecture format (i.e., you listen to lectures to learn knowledge).
My role will be a facilitator who supports your learning. In particular, this course is built on group discussion and collective learning. Most learning will be based on reading assigned materials, discussion, and class activities. I will supplement these activities with short lectures that help contextualize readings, articulate learning themes across weeks, and move the discussion forward.
Learning Activities
Collective Annotation:
For most of the weeks, there is one assigned reading you need to finish reading before coming to the class. You will also be required to make 3 comments on a collective reading document. Your comments will be incorporated into the classroom activity and discussion.
Weekly online discussion
Each week, we are going to have TWO threads of discussion online. The platform we are going to use is
the LinkedIn private group
. The first thread is based on the weekly assigned reading and the collective annotation. The second thread is based on an existing LinkedIn post that is chosen by a designated student. You will be responsible to provide at least ONE response on each thread (meaning TWO responses in total). And you will also have a chance to share one LinkedIn post as our basis of discussion.
The design of this class activity also means each students need to create your own LinkedIn account. The goal is to help students get familiar with the platform and the content on the platform. LinkedIn is also an important source for the course topic – substantiality reporting, carbon accounting, and global environment management and governance.
While the use of LinkedIn in this course is a strategic choice intended to strengthen your learning, you should be mindful of a longer-term consequence of this design. Unlike a comment posted on a course platform that disappears when the semester ends, your contributions in this private LinkedIn group carry a "real stake": they are attached to the professional profile you will take with you into job-seeking, and they may persist beyond this course. This is deliberate. Part of the aim is for you to practice speaking thoughtfully in a professional setting where your name and your words are connected—which is also why participation should be a considered choice, not an afterthought. If you would prefer not to hold a LinkedIn account or not to post under your own name, you may want to avoid enrolling in this course.
Class participation and end-of-class exercise
It is critical to come to the class on time and participate in class activities. My assumption is that a fair proportion of your learning will come from your interaction and collaboration with your classmates during the class. Thus, it is imperative to attend every class except for legitimate reasons (e.g. sick leave or other types of leave permitted by the university).
Collaborative project – Surveying Sustainability Reporting in the Global Higher Education sector
Throughout the semester, our class will collectively produce a critical report on how higher education institutions around the world account for their environmental impacts. Working in groups, you will each analyze sustainability reports from universities in different countries, especially including reports written in languages other than English. We will examine the choices behind them: which frameworks they adopt, how they define what counts, what they measure, and what they leave out. Rather than scoring or ranking universities, our goal is to map the varieties of sustainability reporting practices in the higher education sector and to ask what these documents reveal about how universities understand their environmental responsibilities. More importantly, the goal is not to produce separate analysis by different students but to put together all the analysis as a coherent report. Ideally, we will publicly launch the initial draft of our collective report at the end of the semester. There will be different tasks throughout the semester to craft the report together. I will announce these tasks at the beginning of the semester.
Study Journal:
Study Journal is a Google document you share with me. I will provide detailed instructions later for how to create your Study Journal. I hope this Study Journal will serve as a platform for you to monitor and track your learning progress. It will also be a good way for me to know how you are doing during these four months and what measures I could do to support your learning. You will be responsible for maintaining this Study Journal throughout the 4-month course. In specific, this Study Journal will include four components.
At the beginning of the course, you will need to develop your learning schedule for all the course assignments stated in the syllabus. (mandatory)
In the 9
th
week of the course, you will need to do a mid-term reflection to evaluate your learning so far and how you may adjust your study plan in the next two months. (mandatory)
At the end of the course, you will need to write a brief report evaluating your learning during these four months. (mandatory)
You are welcome to write an update on your learning progress and status any time during the semester (e.g., once a week) on the same document. (optional)

Learning Outcome
During this course, you will have the opportunity to learn how to:
Explain the rationale, structure, and major frameworks of sustainability reporting.
Describe the basic principles of carbon accounting.
Analyze how quantification logic shapes and constrains environmental governance.
Situate sustainability reporting and carbon accounting within their historical and political contexts.
Evaluate the limitations of quantification-based governance and propose alternative approaches.

Engage in a professional learning community by immersing in sustainability trends and discussing with peers on LinkedIn.

The course focuses on digital technology enhanced education innovation and management with applications.
Over the past several years, the field of Educational Technology Management has undergone a significant transformation. The advancements in digital technologies have led to new educational paradigms, and the need for efficient management and effective implementation of these technologies has never been more pressing. This course provides opportunities for students to explore these changes and share experiences and knowledge to improve educational technology management practices.
This course will help students to reflect on the role various forms of electronic and digital technology can play in the teaching/learning
process
and how you can engage these processes in your classroom. Students will become skilled in some of the many digital tools used in today's schools, including MIT’s System Dynamics modelling and simulation-based scenario planning.
This course also consider how a small-scale Educational Technology research project can be conducted in an education
environment
. Case studies and project-based learning with Education for Sustainable Development and organizational learning will be reviewed to offer practical tools and applied research strategies to students prior to conducting their own Educational Technology research project.
課程目標與學習成效:
This course is designed for students to develop their understanding of educational technology and digital empowerment and to learn how to manage educational technologies for better educational practices. Therefore, the objectives of this course are for the student to:
Understand the principles of digital empowerment and trends of educational technology with education innovation issues.
Manage educational technologies for teaching and curriculum development.
Manage educational technologies for e-learning systems.
Develop ideas, steps, and apply digital innovations for organizational learning.
There are three requirements as learning outcomes for students taking this course for a grade.
First, active participation in class discussion is expected. Second, each student must prepare an article review (or case review) and present the articles/case to the class. T
he review should be an analysis of the authors’ theory, methods, and findings. Third, a case study relevant to applications of educational technology and education for sustainable development is required.

英文科目名稱: Analysis and Application of Large-Scale International Survey Data

115-1課表備註: 英文授課。
課程簡介:
Have you ever wondered if people in different countries really live differently? They often think differently about family, work, money, trust, happiness, and politics. They may also behave differently, follow different ways of life, and reach different results in education and health. For example, how many hours do people work, and are shorter working hours linked to more happiness? How do couples share housework across countries? How healthy do people stay as they grow older? And how well do students do in math and science in different school systems and education cultures? In this course, we use real survey data collected from people all around the world to study questions like these.
You will work with several famous international survey projects, including the World Values Survey (WVS), the East Asian Social Survey (EASS), the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP), the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), and the WHO Study on Global AGEing and Adult Health (SAGE).
This course gives you the tools to study that world with real evidence. Step by step, you will learn how these surveys are made, how to clean and prepare the data, how to compare answers fairly across countries, and how to turn your results into a clear report and a short presentation.
You do not need to be a “statistics person” to do well here. We start from the basics and build up slowly. Every new idea comes with a hands-on example, and we review the key statistics together in class before you need to use them. Class demonstrations use R (and Python templates will also be shared), but you may use any software you like for your own work, including R, Python, Stata, SAS, or SPSS. There are no required prerequisites. Having taken (or currently taking) an introductory statistics or research methods course is helpful, but it is not mandatory.
The skills you build here are useful far beyond the classroom and beyond academic research. You will learn how to work with large and messy real-world data, how to ask a clear question and find the answer in the numbers, how to make simple charts and tables that tell a story, and how to explain your findings to people who are not experts.
課程目標與學習成效:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
Understand how the major international surveys (WVS, EASS, ISSP, PISA, and SAGE) are built, and why they are useful for studying how people think, behave, live, and learn in different countries.
Prepare and clean real survey data, and run basic to intermediate analysis using the software of your choice.
Ask a clear research question and test it with care, while watching for common problems in comparing countries (for example, sampling, and whether a question means the same thing in each country).
Write and present your own short research that compares countries or studies a topic in an international setting.
Turn data into a clear story: make simple charts and tables, draw honest conclusions, and explain your findings to people who are not experts.

課程簡介: This course introduces the foundational concepts and practical approaches in public policy analysis and advocacy. Public policy is any decisions and actions (or indecisions and inactions) of governments. Public policy analysis is a tool to inform policymakers’ decisions, and policy advocacy is the technique to engage with stakeholders and communicate with the public to pursue policy change. This course will cover key stages in policy analysis and advocacy, such as problem identification, policy formulation, decision-making, advocacy, and adoption. Through case-based learning and theoretical grounding, students will explore how policy problems are defined, options developed and evaluated, and stakeholder interests negotiated. Explain core concepts in public policy, including problem definition, policy formulation, and the adoption process.

Communicate policy ideas and proposals effectively through both oral and written formats to inform policymakers and the public.

課程簡介:
Course Description:
The legal regime regulating the rights and obligations of States in their use of the seas has long been one of the most dynamic and important areas of International law. Various economic activities of humankind take place in the seas and oceans, and, at times, they are also hot spots for regional tensions and conflicts. The law of the sea provides the legal framework reflected in the wealth of customary laws, treaty laws, and judicial opinions dealing with this subject.
This course provides a full picture of the legal framework of the state practice in the seas, mainly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Emphasis will be given on the issues of state sovereignty and their sovereign rights in maritime zones, due regard when when states exercise maritime freedom and rights, mechanism of dispute settlement, and enviroment aspects regarding climate change and living resources. Law enforcement and military activities on the seas will also be equally addressed, among others.
The theories and state practice will be introduced through the rulings of international judicial bodies and academic treatises. Students will have a chance to examine the balance of rights and interests between states and between states and the international community and identify the challenges to the legal framework from emerging issues on environment protection, climate change, and maritime security.

In recent years, Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an important tool for solving social problems. However, due to its ongoing development, many gaps still need to be filled to meet the professional requirements of various industries. This course aims to train students to utilize the latest technologies in Generative AI and data science to develop projects that can address real-world challenges. The technology covered includes, but is not limited to, diverse content (such as text, audio, and video) connections, fine-tuning, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

In the second section, partner organizations will present AI projects based on current industry needs and define the objectives of each project. In the third section, students will follow detailed guidelines provided by instructors and professional mentors to complete their assigned projects.

Course Description
Contemporary society seems to be grappling with numerous crises and challenges! In 2000, United Nations member states collectively signed the Millennium Declaration, aiming to tackle major global issues such as poverty and hunger through collaborative efforts. In a similar vein, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation launched the Grand Challenges initiative in 2003, seeking to identify significant contemporary challenges and promote the development of innovative solutions. Coinciding with this, in 2008, the U.S. National Academy of Engineering announced 14 Grand Challenges for engineering, aimed at driving research to solve complex and intractable social problems, often referred to as "wicked social problems." Following this approach, the European Union in 2014 identified seven major societal challenges to guide technological development policies. Finally, in 2015, the United Nations updated the global challenges and introduced the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), outlining seventeen major challenges that the global community should overcome by 2030. It is evident that the international community increasingly relies on the concept of "Grand Challenges" to define and address the various social problems facing humanity.
As the world confronts various "Grand Challenges," there is a growing tendency to look toward potential "innovations" as solutions to these global crises. Increasing resources are being allocated to promote diverse innovations aimed at addressing these significant challenges. This reliance on technological advancements to solve major social issues is also reflected in international policy-making. In 2014, the European Union introduced the Horizon 2020 research and innovation program, with the primary objective of using "Responsible Research and Innovation" to tackle key societal challenges. Similarly, in 2015, when the United Nations unveiled the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), it also released a policy white paper detailing how science, technology, and innovation (STI) can be harnessed to achieve these goals.
Various issues arise following this trend. What are these innovations being promoted by international agencies? How could we discern whether these innovations could really solve the social and environmental problems without unintended consequences? In short, how could we develop a deeper understanding of these innovations as solutions to global problems?
These are questions that constitute the basis of this course. In this course, relying on perspectives from different disciplines in social sciences, we are going to collectively explore the landscape of innovation in the international development field. We will also learn to develop various analytical tools to assess potential and existing innovations poised to solve grand challenges.

Class Activity & Group Discussion & Short Lecture:
I employ a
student-centered learning approach
in this course rather than a traditional lecture format (i.e., you listen to lectures to learn knowledge).
My role will be a facilitator who supports your learning. In particular, this course is built on group discussion and collective learning. Most learning will be based on reading assigned materials, discussion, and class activities. I will supplement these activities with short lectures that help contextualize readings, articulate learning themes across weeks, and move the discussion forward.

My assumption is that a fair proportion of your learning will come from your interaction and collaboration with your classmates during the class. Throughout the course, you will also need to pair with the other student and investigate a specific innovation in Taiwan beyond the semiconductor sector. At the end of the semester, each group of students will need to produce a 3000-word piece of essay. Your essay will have the chance to be included in a special issue in the

To prepare each group to work on your case study, we will learn a series of analytical questions and different kinds of “stakeholder analysis” mapping tools that could allow you to carry out the analysis. You will also have the opportunity to carry out some fieldwork to study the case better.

The Innovation This Week:
To facilitate you to cultivate familiarity with innovations across the global development arena and develop tools and skills to stay connected with the global world, I developed this learning activity called “The Innovation This Week.” Everyone will rotate to share the background of one specific innovation. I will give you a more specific guideline during the class.
Study Journal:
Study Journal is a Google document you share with me. I will provide detailed instructions later for how to create your Study Journal. I hope this Study Journal will serve as a platform for you to monitor and track your learning progress. It will also be a good way for me to know how you are doing during these four months and what measures I could do to support your learning. You will be responsible for maintaining this Study Journal throughout the 4-month course. In specific, this Study Journal will include four components.

課程簡介:
The notion of Gaia-politics challenges traditional approaches to sovereignty by taking more seriously the geo of geopolitics, that is to say its environmental dimension. War ecology is another concept that aims to address the concomitance of the climate emergency with more traditional threats on national security including military and civilian defense. Through guess lectures, off campus visits and negotiation theaters, the class focuses on the case of Taiwan in comparison with other countries.
In 2023, this course focused on conflicts between humans and non-humans. In 2024, we paid attention to the role of social movements (such as environmental protection and antinuclear mobilization), and how they connect with national politics, in particular state agencies and the parliament. In 2025, we explored with a critical eye the catchwords of ‘social resilience’, ‘technological innovation’ and ‘energy transition’, and how these effectively influence collective preparation to climate change and war scenarios.
In 2026, while continuing our research on these topics, we will also conduct an educational experiment that requires us to spend most of our time out of the classroom. The idea is to take a pause, detox from our overuse of electronics and AI, and return to the basics of ethnographic fieldwork with our eyes and ears wide open, using handwritten notes and drawings.
「蓋婭政治」(Gaia-politics)的概念挑戰了「主權」 概念的傳統取徑，因為蓋婭政治更認真看待「地緣政治」中的「地緣」，也就是其環境面向。「戰爭生態學」(war ecology)則是另一個概念，旨在面對氣候緊急狀態與傳統國安威脅(包括軍事與民間防 衛)共存的局勢。
透過客座課程、校外參訪與協商劇場的形式，本課 程將聚焦於台灣相較於其他國家的情勢。2023年， 本課程聚焦於人類與非人類之間的衝突。2024年， 我們更注重社會運動(如環保與反核運動)的角 色，以及它們如何與國內政治——特別是政府機構與國會——產生連結。
2025年，我們將在延續對跨物種正義、社會運動與 國家政治的關注之餘，進一步批判性地探討「社會 韌性」、「科技創新」與「能源轉型」這些關鍵詞，並檢視它們如何實質地影響集體面對氣候變遷與戰爭 情境的準備與應對能力。
2026年，我們除了將繼續探索上述議題，亦會將多數時間移至教室之外，進行一項教育性實驗計畫。本計畫旨在按下暫停鍵，戒斷我們對3C產品與人工智慧的過度使用；並以敏銳的觀察與傾聽，透過手寫與手繪紀錄，回歸民族誌田野工作的基礎。
課程目標與學習成效:
The goal of this mixed-method approach—using ethnographic fieldwork and negotiation theater—is to improve our capacity to detach from electronic devices and increase our focus while reading scientific papers, attending lectures, participating in group discussions, and conducting ethnographic fieldwork. In other words, this means listening and observing, taking valuable notes, and turning these observations into social capital and political will through class discussions. Meanwhile, protests against the environmental cost of electronic waste and the huge carbon footprint of AI data centers provide further reminders and incentives to detox from electronics. Last but not least, as Taiwan’s civil defense organizations train their members, we must also learn to cope with electricity shortages or blackouts in the event of a military emergency, natural hazard, or industrial disaster (such as earthquakes, typhoons, or gas explosions).
課程目標與預期成果：本課程透過民族誌田野工作與協商劇場的混合途徑，旨在幫助我們降低對電子產品的依賴，藉此提升在閱讀文獻、參與講座、小組討論與田野工作時的專注力。具體而言，我們將練習觀察與傾聽、作好筆記，並透過課堂討論將這些觀察轉化為社會資本與政治動能。此外，遠離 3C 也是對當前社會與環境議題的反思。電子垃圾的環境代價與 AI 資料中心的巨大碳足跡，不斷提醒並促使我們減少對電子設備的依賴。最後，正如台灣民防組織對其會員的訓練，我們也必須透過這門課學會：在遭遇軍事衝突或天災人禍（如地震、颱風、氣爆）時，如何面對並適應缺電或停電的狀態。

課程簡介:
International organisations (IOs) have been created over the past century to advance cooperation among states to find common solutions to international and transnational challenges. IOs are tools of international politics and international relations, while serving as indispensable fora for establishing and implementing international norms and principles. Some of the key international challenges tackled by IOs include armed conflicts, humanitarian crises, infectious diseases, climate change, international trade and global inequality. IOs vary greatly in terms of their mission, functions, membership, structure, powers and geographical scope. The role of IOs in international politics remains controversial: while some perceive them as enablers to achieving global solutions beyond the capacity of individual states, others question their effectiveness and legitimacy given their tendency to be controlled by the most powerful states. States and citizens alike are sometimes disappointed by the gap between IOs’ lofty aspirations and their actual performance in addressing global problems.
The course will start by introducing the central analytical approaches that help students understand key characteristics of international organisations: their creation and design, their power and mandates, their decision-making processes, their impact and policy effectiveness, and their interaction with states and other IOs. This analytical framework is then applied to analyse the functions and performance of IOs concerning specific global challenges and policy domains, including peace, security, human rights, trade, crisis response, health and environment. Finally, the course will examine the responsibility and accountability of IOs, and examine the geopolitical realities that limit Taiwan’s participation in these international fora.
The course will be taught by Associate Professor Kevin Chang (JD, LLM, MA, GradDipIntLaw, GradDipLegPrac, BSc), who is a senior advisor on international law and who brings more than 20 years’ experience as a lawyer, advocate and practitioner with the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the Australian Government and other international organisations. Professor Chang is a Lawyer of the Supreme Court of the Australian Capital Territory. He also teaches at the University of Sydney and the Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies in Geneva.
This course will be taught via a hybrid mode of teaching of 50% being in-person, the other 50% online. Students are expected to read the prescribed reading material in advance, submit reflection notes, and participate in class discussions. This course is designed with an assumption that students will already have a solid appreciation of international politics. This course is suitable only for students who have an advanced level of English proficiency. Because of the class size limit of 25 students, prospective students may be required to submit a statement of motivation prior to their enrolment being confirmed.
課程目標與學習成效: The key aim of this course is to gain a deep understanding of IOs and their capacities for solving the world’s greatest challenges. Students will gain detailed knowledge of IOs through analysis of their characteristics, powers, legitimacy and performance, and will recognise the promises and limitations of IOs in the modern global system. Students will understand the powers possessed by IOs, as well as challenges faced by them, through examining their performance with respect to major global issues and crises.

The course is also tentatively planned to include an innovative learning method called “Learning Together”: in one of the weeks, our students will be learning together with students from NTNU’s Department of East Asia Studies. This will be done either by receiving NTNU’s students in our classroom or by visiting NTNU’s class on politics in Southeast Asia.
The course “Hybrid Regimes: Democratic Challenges in Southeast Asia” is designed as a standalone course or as a follow-up course for students who have completed the introductory course “Politics in Southeast Asia: Change and Continuity”. The course examines the socio-political development of authoritarian and hybrid regimes in Asia, enabling students to survey, compare, and analyze the persistent challenges of democratization in the region. While the empirical focus is Southeast Asia, the course also situates regional political dynamics within broader geopolitical relations, particularly with East Asian actors such as China, Taiwan, and Japan. Cambodia’s limited democratization, for instance, has been analyzed by some scholars in relation to its close ties with China. From this perspective, democratization in Southeast Asia may also be influenced by engagement with consolidated democracies, such as Taiwan and Japan.
The course further engages with Taiwan’s foreign policy initiative, the NEW SOUTHBOUND POLICY, through which Taiwan seeks to deepen economic, political, and cultural relations with Southeast Asian countries.
In the aftermath of the Cold War, a global wave of democratization reshaped political systems across Asia, Central and Eastern Europe, Latin America, and Sub-Saharan Africa. The dissolution of the Soviet Union weakened the legitimacy of many authoritarian regimes, leading to transitions toward multiparty systems and liberal reforms. However, regime transitions did not always result in democratic consolidation, and many states experienced stalled or reversed democratization processes.
While pure authoritarian regimes have become less common in Asia, many states are better understood as “hybrid regimes” or “electoral autocracies”, positioned between liberal democracy and authoritarian rule. These regimes typically maintain the formal structures of electoral competition, including multiparty elections, while systematically limiting opposition voices through institutional manipulation, uneven political competition, and selective enforcement of rules. In these nations, the thin veneer of quasi-democratic institutions and multi-party elections became a façade for abuses of power, manipulation and corruption. In Thailand, following the 2019 election, the military-backed government dissolved an opposition party and arrested activists, triggering widespread student-led protests demanding constitutional reform and greater civil liberties. In 2023, although the opposition Move Forward Party won the election, it was prevented from forming a government due to institutional constraints and entrenched political interests. In the Philippines in 2016, voter dissatisfaction with crime and entrenched elite politics contributed to the election of Rodrigo Duterte, whose administration was associated with an extensive “war on drugs” involving extrajudicial killings. In 2022, voters elected Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the son and namesake of the former dictator, signaling the persistence of dynastic politics. In Myanmar, the military coup in 2021 marked a reversal of electoral democratization and a return to direct military rule.
The course also incorporates analysis of the role of digital technologies in shaping political competition and state-society relations in Southeast Asia
.
Social media platforms have become central arenas for electoral mobilization, political communication, and contestation in hybrid regimes.
Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), further amplify these dynamics by enabling new forms of political communication and information manipulation at scale.
In several cases, coordinated online networks, including troll activities and disinformation campaigns, were deployed during election periods to influence public opinion and delegitimize opposition actors. Concurrently,
states have introduced regulatory frameworks such as anti-fake news legislation and cybersecurity laws, which, while formally justified in terms of public order and information integrity, may also function as instruments of digital surveillance
and constraints on freedom of expression. These developments underscore how hybrid regimes are sustained not only through formal institutions and coercive mechanisms, but also through digital infrastructures and information environments.
Some of the questions the course seeks to answer are: What is democracy good for? Why do some states democratize while others continue to exhibit authoritarianism? How do highly corrupt political regimes survive for decades? How do populist leaders gain and maintain power in Asia? What is the legacy of political violence in newly democratic states? What is the legacy of military rule in the region? How do global human rights values and “Asian values” shape political development in the region? How do digital technologies, including social media platforms, disinformation networks, and state regulatory frameworks, reshape political competition, state-society relations, and the boundaries of free expression in hybrid regimes? 課程簡介:
International trade is the economic backbone of most countries in the world. The development of information technologies has pushed forward the trade facilitation and digitalization of cross border exchange. The digital transformation of international trade has reduced the operation time and costs, facilitated the global value chain, and connected the trade and logistics communities globally.
Cross border digital trade attracts higher attention than ever in the post COVID-19 era. While normal international trade procedures and operations which are heavily dependent on paper-documents are interrupted, the use of technologies helps to make the international trade more resilient and lower the barriers of physical documentation. International initiatives as well as respective government’s actions in the implementation of cross border digital trade to increase the scale, scope and speed of trade will be introduced in this course. Challenges including the adoption of new technologies, policy and regulation issues, change of user behavior during the implementation of cross border digital trade will also be discussed in the course.
This course aims to develop students’ knowledge about the digitalization of international trade for increasing their competitive edges in the global business setting.
